quote: Was bedeutet Jacobis Umkehrproblem und was das Abelsche Theorem für $p = \infty$.
english: What does Jacobi's inversion problem mean, and what does Abel's theorem mean, for p = ∞?
topic: Notes posing several problems: expanding e^π = i^i into a simple continued fraction, a reduction of a problem of Lindemann's to finding rational functions invariant under a substitution, the meaning of Jacobi's inversion problem and Abel's theorem for genus p = ∞, and the behaviour of the second root when a root is approximated by a quadratic equation.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert asks how the classical theory of compact Riemann surfaces (algebraic curves) of finite genus p carries over when the genus is infinite. The theory in question is Abel's theorem, which characterizes divisors of meromorphic functions through the Abel–Jacobi map into the Jacobian C^p/Λ, and Jacobi's inversion problem, which asks to invert the Abel map on p-fold symmetric products. In modern terms: for a suitable class of open Riemann surfaces of infinite genus (for example hyperelliptic surfaces with infinitely many branch points), can one define an Abel map into an infinite-dimensional 'Jacobian' torus and theta functions? Do analogues of Abel's theorem, Jacobi inversion and related results hold? This is a genuine but programmatic research question, not a single precise conjecture.
triage.answered_by: No source found links Hilbert's note to later work, and I found no evidence that he published it as a problem. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th. The question was later taken up independently in the theory of infinite-genus Riemann surfaces. H. P. McKean and E. Trubowitz built hyperelliptic function theory with infinitely many branch points (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 29, 1976, pp. 143–226) and theta functions for 'Hill's surfaces' (Bull. AMS 84, 1978). J. Feldman, H. Knörrer and E. Trubowitz then set out a general class of infinite-genus Riemann surfaces to which the classical theory, up to and including the Torelli theorem, extends (CRM Monograph Series vol. 20, AMS, 2003). Solving the infinite-genus Jacobi inversion problem is a known tool for periodic KdV solutions.

evidence.claim: McKean & Trubowitz, 'Hill's operator and hyperelliptic function theory in the presence of infinitely many branch points', Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 29 (1976), no. 2, 143–226.
McKean & Trubowitz, 'Hill's surfaces and their theta functions', Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 84 (1978), 1042–1085.
Feldman, Knörrer and Trubowitz introduce a class of infinite-genus Riemann surfaces to which the classical theory of compact Riemann surfaces, up to and including the Torelli theorem, extends.

The monograph 'Riemann Surfaces of Infinite Genus' (CRM Monograph Series 20, AMS) covers L^2-cohomology, theta series, the Torelli theorem, hyperelliptic, heat and Fermi surfaces of infinite genus, and the KP equation.

For infinite-gap potentials, computing the map from spectral variables to the infinite-genus torus requires solving an infinite-genus Jacobi inversion problem. Its solvability gives existence, uniqueness and qualitative results for periodic KdV solutions (IMRN 2021).

triage.why: The note is a short, open-ended question rather than a sharp conjecture, and I found no source connecting it to Hilbert. Mathematically, though, it matches a well-developed later theory: infinite-genus versions of Abel's theorem and Jacobi inversion. McKean and Trubowitz started this in 1976–78, motivated by Hill's operator and KdV, and Feldman, Knörrer and Trubowitz carried it through to the Torelli theorem in 2003. The field is still active in integrable systems (KdV/KP and infinite-gap potentials, e.g. IMRN 2021). The verdict is 'solved' in the sense that answers now exist for natural classes of surfaces. No general answer for arbitrary infinite-genus surfaces is claimed, which is why confidence is medium.
